about: The city's calendar and memory (urbs_town.gd): the week and its market day, the festivals of a short year, what happens at set hours (processions, a speech from the Rostra, the crier), rain, what people say to each other, gossip, favours, the sounds of the trades, and the regulars you come to know across the ages. {a} and {b} are two people's names, {other} and {title} someone you have met.

festivals.name: the Saturnalia
festivals.news: It's the Saturnalia! No work, gifts, dice in the street, and the slaves sit at table with their masters. Io Saturnalia!
cries: Io Saturnalia!
Dice in the open, and no aedile to stop it!
Today the slaves eat first. Tomorrow they don't.
Drink, it's the Saturnalia!

festivals.name: the Lupercalia
festivals.news: The Lupercalia! The young men run round the Palatine in goatskins and strike the women with thongs, for luck with children.
cries: Here they come, the Luperci!
Strike me, for a child this year!
Round the Palatine, naked as wolves!

festivals.name: the Parilia, Rome's birthday
festivals.news: The Parilia today: Rome's birthday. Bonfires tonight, and the shepherds leap over them.
cries: Jump the fire, for purity!
Happy birthday, Rome!
Straw for the fires!

festivals.name: the Roman Games
festivals.news: The Roman Games! Races in the Circus all week. The whole city's going.
cries: To the Circus!
Red! Red! Put a curse on the Whites!
Seats! Seats for a copper!

festivals.name: Easter
festivals.news: Easter. Christ is risen. The new Christians are baptised tonight, all in white.
cries: Christ is risen!
Alleluia!
To the church, quickly!
Ah! Ah! Ah!
He was thirty-one.
Make way for the dead!
Who'll feed his children now?
Talasse! Talasse!
Hymen, Hymenaee!
She's fourteen. He's forty. A good match, they say.
Lift her over the threshold, don't let her stumble!
Favete linguis! Keep holy silence!
A white ox for the god!
Garlands! Garlands!

republic: Citizens! The Senate buys your votes and starves your children!
Who paid you to stand there, Rufus?
Grain! Grain before games!
Pompey's soldiers in the Forum! Is this the Republic?
empire: Citizens, the Emperor's generosity feeds you all!
Praise to the Senate and the Roman people!
(muttering) Say it louder, he's paying.
late: The city has its walls and its bread. Be grateful!
The Emperor in the east thinks of Rome!
(a voice) Then let him send bread!
early: Citizens! Carthage is beaten. Now beware the softness that comes with victory!
The Republic keeps faith: land for every man who served!
Remember Cannae. Remember who did not ask for peace!
heroic: Citizens! Pyrrhus asks for peace. Appius says: no peace while a king stands in Italy!
The Samnites are our allies now. Honour them as Romans!
Every man to his century when the trumpet sounds!
collapse: Citizens! The new Emperor, chosen for us by the Goths of Toulouse, greets you!
Games! There will be games for his accession!
(a voice) How long will this one last?

republic: Auction at the Temple of Castor! A house on the Carinae!
Lost! A slave boy, Syrian, answers to Eros!
empire: Games at the Amphitheatre, the Kalends! Fifty pairs of gladiators!
Auction! Wine from Campania, a hundred jars!
late: By order of the Prefect: bread at the steps at the ninth hour!
Races at the Circus! Greens against Blues!
collapse: Races on the Ides! Greens against Blues!
Auction of the goods of the late Emperor's friends!

republic: It's market day! The country's come to town!
Chickens! Eggs! Cheese from Tusculum!
empire: Market day! Everything from the farms!
Honey! Fresh honey!
late: Market day, what there is of it.
Beans, cheap!
early: Market day! The farms are back, and the men with them!
Grain from Sicily, cheap at last!
heroic: Market day! Beans, barley, a good ox!
Salt from Ostia! Salt!
collapse: Market day. What's left.
No grain. Beans, dear.

late: Bread for the poor, one each!
God bless the bishop!
fall: Bread from the Pope's farms! One loaf each!
Wait your turn!
collapse: Bread for the poor, one each!
God bless the bishop!

republic: Fresh from Gaul, strong backs, taken this summer! Chalk on their feet, placards round their necks, read them!
A girl, fifteen, Greek, can read and sew! Healthy! Do I hear two thousand?
A cook, trained! Warranted not a runaway!
empire: Syrians, Thracians, a Briton! Warranted sound!
A scribe, Greek, writes a fair hand! Three thousand!
Two boys, brothers, sold together or apart!
late: A Goth, taken on the Danube! Strong!
A girl, twelve, from Cappadocia!
Cheap today, the war's brought plenty!

cries: Out to the Esquiline gate with him!
A slave who struck his master.
Don't look, children, don't look.
The birds will have him by tomorrow.

republic: Out! The rent was due at the Kalends!
Where will we go? The baby's sick!
Take the bed, take the pots, that settles half of it.
empire: By the owner's order, out by noon!
We've lived here nine years!
The furniture's forfeit. The door's forfeit.
late: Out, all of you!
The Church will take us, or nobody will.
Sell the loom, it's all we have.
collapse: Out, all of you!
The Church will take us, or nobody will.
Sell the loom, it's all we have.

republic: Water! Buckets, from the fountain!
The top floors! Nobody got down from the top floors!
The speculators are here already, offering to buy the block while it burns.
empire: The vigiles! Pull the wall down before it spreads!
My children were on the fifth floor!
Blankets, vinegar, here!
late: Fire in the Subura!
Get the old man out!
It's all gone. Everything.
collapse: Fire in the Subura!
Get the old man out!
It's all gone. Everything.

republic: Two asses, handsome.
Come in out of the street.
Not him, he never pays.
empire: Two asses. Come in.
The room's warm.
Mind the pimp, he's in a mood.
late: Two asses.
Come in, come in.
The priests walk past quicker every year.
collapse: Two asses.
Come in, come in.
The priests walk past quicker every year.

republic: Bread! Bread or blood!
The ships are late, the prices are up, and the Senate eats!
Stone them! Stone the aedile!
late: Bread! The Prefect hoards it!
Burn the Prefect's house!
The soldiers are coming!
collapse: Bread! The Prefect hoards it!
Burn the Prefect's house!
The soldiers are coming!

cries: Io triumphe! Io triumphe!
Africanus! Africanus!
Carthage's silver, look, the wagons of it!
The slave in the chariot whispers to him: remember you are mortal.
The legions of Cannae, home at last!
The masks of his ancestors walk before him: consuls, censors, men who triumphed!
He fell at Zama at the head of his century.
His son will speak his deeds from the Rostra, and the young men will listen.
A good death. A Roman death.

events.speaker: praeco
cries: The levy! Tribe by tribe, every man of age!
Swear it: to follow the consul, not to desert, not to leave the ranks except to save a Roman or take up a weapon.
I'm seventeen. Take me.
My father served. His father served. Write my name.

heroic: And Horatius said: two of you, stand with me, and we'll hold them while the bridge falls!
Mucius put his right hand in the fire and didn't flinch. The king let him go. Left-hand, they called him after.
Decius veiled his head, stood on a spear, spoke the words, and rode into the Gauls. And the gods took him.
Curius, turnips, the Samnite gold! Ha! Tell it again!

cries: South, to Pyrrhus!
Come back with your shield or on it!
Mars go with you, my son!
Elephants! We'll see about elephants!

collapse: A thread from the tunic of the Apostle! Genuine!
A bone of Saint Laurence, blessed, cures fever!
Charms against Vandals! Two for one!
Three to one the new one's dead by the spring!
Greens! Greens! The Blues' horses are cursed!
Who cares who's emperor, who's driving for the Greens?

events.speaker: meretrix
cries: Under the arches, handsome. Two asses.
Fornix, they call this. It's a living.
Not that one, he's the watch's cousin.
Cold tonight. Come in under the vault.

events.speaker: mango
cries: A Cappadocian! Strong as an ox, thirty years, no vices, I swear it on my mother!
Chalked feet, fresh off the boat at Puteoli. Look at his teeth. Look!
Reads and writes Greek, this one, keeps accounts. Two thousand, and I lose on it.
Jump. Jump, I said. See? Sound in wind and limb.
A girl of sixteen, a Syrian, sings. Bids start at eight hundred.
Sold to the gentleman in the striped tunic.

events.speaker: caupo
cries: Another cup, Fortunata! Water it less this time!
I can't feel my legs. Where are my legs?
Hnnngh... oh gods. Oh gods.
Dice! Who's for dice? The Venus throw wins the pot!
Six! Six! Pay up, you dog!
The Saturnalia was better in my father's day.
Sing, you bastards! Sing!

events.speaker: proletarius
cries: Knife! He's got a knife!
Thief! Stop him!
The watch! Someone call the watch!
Hold him down! Hold him!
Leave it. Leave it, he's done for.
Nobody saw anything. Nobody.
Rain. Under the portico.
The gutters will flood the low streets tonight.
There goes the washing.
The Tiber'll be up by morning. Mind the low flats.

early: Salve, {b}. Your son's home?
Home, {a}, with a scar and a land grant. The gods be thanked.
Did you see the triumph?
I saw it. I wept. My brother should have been in it.
They say the young men want Greek cooks now.
Let them try it in this street. My father ate turnips and beat the Samnites.
The levy's called again.
Then we'll answer, {a}. Same as always.
You owe me for the grain, {b}.
By the Kalends. You have my word. That's enough for me.
The Senate's giving land in Apulia.
The Republic keeps faith. It always has.
republic: Salve, {b}. Paid your rent?
Half of it, {a}. The other half's a promise.
Who are you voting for?
Whoever's paying most. Same as you.
Did you hear about the fire on the Esquiline?
Three floors. The landlord was at his villa. Nobody from the top got out.
Clodius's men were in the Subura last night.
Milo's will be here tonight. Stay in.
Remember when a Roman's word was worth something?
My grandfather did. He's dead.
There was a body by the fountain this morning.
Knifed. Nobody saw anything. Nobody ever does.
empire: Going to the games?
What else is there to do?
Careful, {b}. That one's an informer.
They're all informers now, {a}.
They sold Syrus.
After twenty years in the house? To some farm in Apulia. Chained gangs.
My cousin's selling her daughter to a household on the Palatine.
Better than starving. At least she'll eat.
Your boy's joined the legions?
Twenty-five years on the frontier. For pay. Nobody joins for Rome now.
The Emperor gave another dole.
And another games. We're fed like his dogs, {a}.
late: The tax men came again.
They took the seed grain. What do we plant?
They tortured a man at the Prefect's today. Tax arrears.
Don't talk about it. Walk.
My son can't leave the bakers' guild. It's the law.
Chained to the oven. Like a slave, {a}.
Did you pray at the church or the temple?
Both. Whichever one's watching.
The price of bread!
Don't, {a}. Just don't.
fall: Have you eaten?
Not since yesterday.
The Goths are gone.
Till the next ones.
They took the lead off the roofs of the baths.
Let them. Nobody bathes.
My mother died in the night.
Mine in the siege. Bury her by the church, they'll say a prayer.
heroic: Salve, {b}! The beans are good this year.
And the barley, {a}! The gods are pleased with us.
Heard about Pyrrhus's elephants?
Big grey oxen with noses for tails. We'll manage.
Your boy's off to the legions?
With his father's shield and his grandfather's spear, {a}.
The Greek at the inn says we're barbarians.
The Greek at the inn owes me for his dinner.
Is it true Fabricius sent the king's doctor back in chains?
He did! The doctor offered to poison Pyrrhus. Fabricius wouldn't win like that.
collapse: Did you see him? The new Emperor?
Which one? There's been three since Easter.
The Vandals took the roof of Jupiter.
It was gilded. What did Jupiter ever do for us?
My wife sold our daughter's dowry for grain.
Mine sold our daughter.
The Senate met today.
About what? The order of seating at the games.
Bet on the Greens?
On the Greens, the Emperor, the end of the world. Why not.

early: {other} the {title}? Lost two sons at Cannae and sent the third to Scipio. A Roman family.
{other}, the {title}. Honest as the day. Never once broke his word, they say.
{other} the {title}? Too fond of Greek ways, some say. Mind you, he fought well enough.
republic: You met {other}? The {title}? Owes money to a lender on the Sacred Way. The kind who sends men round.
{other} the {title}? Sold their vote twice at the last election, to both sides.
{other}. The {title}. Their {kin} sleeps elsewhere most nights, and everyone knows where but them.
empire: {other} the {title} is an informer. I'm not saying. I'm just saying, watch what you tell them.
{other} the {title}? Buried two children this year. Doesn't talk about it.
{other} the {title} was a slave until two years ago. Look at the airs on them now.
late: {other} the {title}? Paid off the tax collector. With what, I'd like to know.
{other} the {title} goes to church in the morning and the old shrine at night.
fall: {other} the {title}? Still alive, then. That's news.
{other} the {title} ate things in the siege nobody should eat. Don't ask.
heroic: {other} the {title}? Fought at Sentinum, three wounds, all in front. A good man.
{other}, the {title}. Their grandmother was a Sabine. Makes the best bread in the street.
{other} the {title}? Talks too much about the Greeks. Harmless, mind.
collapse: {other} the {title}? Sold the lead off their own roof to the Vandals' agents. Rain comes in now.
{other} the {title} bought a bishop's favour and a senator's daughter in the same week.
{other} the {title}? They'll be dead or rich by summer. Nobody in between any more.

asks: Do me a kindness, stranger. Tell {target}, the {title}, that {msg}. They'll know what it means.
If you pass {target} the {title}, tell them {msg}. I can't leave the shop.
messages: the lender wants his money by the Ides
his brother's been taken by the watch
the landlord's men are coming tomorrow
the fever's in the house, keep the children away
don't come to the tavern tonight, you know why
thanks: {from} sent you? Gods. Thank you. I'll go now.
From {from}? Then it's worse than I thought. Thank you, stranger.
after: You told {target}? Good. You're decent, for a foreigner.
Thank you for the message. It came in time. This time.

republic: Felix, baker, like my father. The oven, the mill, three slaves, and the loan I took to buy them.
My girl's to be married at the Kalends. Fourteen. He's a good man, a fuller, twice her age. I'm baking the cake myself.
She died in childbirth, in the spring. The boy lived. He's with us now. I bake at night so I don't have to think.
empire: Numisius Felix. Four generations in this bakery. My great-great-grandfather raised his grandson here when his daughter died.
The state buys our bread for the dole. Steady money, and the guild tells us what to charge and whom to hire.
We put the family name on the lintel in marble. So it outlasts us.
late: Numisia. I run the bakery: my husband's dead, and the law binds bakers' children to the trade. My sons can't leave it if they want to.
The guild owns us now more than we own it. The Prefect's men count every loaf.
The name over the door says Felix. Nobody remembers who he was.
fall: See that doorway? A bakery, once. The Felixes, four hundred years of them, they say.
The last of them starved in the siege, with the rest of the street.
Spare a crust, stranger? For the old baker's sake.
early: Numisius, baker, as my father was. My elder son fell at Cannae. The younger is home from Zama with a land grant. I bake for both of them now.
My girl's betrothed to a veteran of Scipio's. A good man. He has a scar across his face and he's not ashamed of it, nor is she.
The Felix name will be on this oven when Rome is a thousand years old. I believe that.
heroic: Numisius. Four iugera outside the Colline Gate, a wife, three boys, a plough. What more does a Roman want?
My eldest was at Sentinum when Decius rode out. He came home with a scar and a story, and he tells it every night.
One day there'll be a Numisius in the Senate, you'll see. Or at least a Numisius with more than four iugera.
collapse: Numisia. The Vandals took the flour and the donkeys. The oven's cold. The name's still over the door.
My son joined a barbarian general's household guard. Better paid than the Emperor's.
They sell relics where the mill was. Bones and cloth. Nobody wants bread they can't afford.

regulars.habit: as my father used to say

republic: Hilarus. Twelve fights, twelve alive. Three more and they give me the wooden sword.
Fourteen. The last one was a boy from the same school. We shared bread for a year. The crowd wanted it finished.
Free, with the wooden sword. And a hand that won't close, and a leg that won't bend. I'll open a tavern. What else is there?
empire: Callistus. Net and trident. The crowd likes a retiarius who loses slowly.
Hilarus's tavern, in the Subura? My grandfather drank there. The old Thracian's scars were a legend.
Twenty-one fights. I've stopped counting the men. The emperor nodded to me once.
late: Nicias. The emperors don't like the games now, and the bishops call it murder. They're not wrong. It was my life.
Now I train men for the beast hunts. The beasts don't pray.
When I'm gone, nobody will know how it was done. Maybe that's for the best.
early: Varenus. First spear of my legion at Zama. Sixteen years under arms. I was at Cannae too, and I lived, and they sent us to Sicily in disgrace.
Scipio took the Cannae men to Africa and let us wash it out in Hannibal's blood. We did.
Land in Apulia, and an oak crown from a man whose life I saved. I'd go again tomorrow.
heroic: Pomponius. Hastatus in the front line. I've fought Samnites, Etruscans, Umbrians and Gauls, and married a Samnite. Life's funny.
At Sentinum I saw Decius veil his head. I've never been so frightened or so proud.
Now it's Pyrrhus. Elephants, phalanx, all very Greek. We'll see how they like a Roman line.

republic: Caecilius Rufus. My family has held the consulship four times. This year I'm buying a praetorship for my son. The price is outrageous.
Clodius's gangs, Milo's gangs, Pompey's soldiers in the Forum. Is this still the Republic? I vote with whoever will leave my estates alone.
My son won the praetorship. We're in debt for twenty years. He'll get a province and make it back, one way or another.
empire: Caecilius Rufus. My family ran the Republic. Now we agree beautifully with the Emperor, and keep our heads.
A cousin was denounced last year. An informer, a lie about a statue. His estates went to the treasury. He opened his veins.
The Emperor asked my advice. I gave the answer he wanted. That's what advice is now.
late: Caecilius Rufus. We keep the old gods at home, quietly. The laws forbid the sacrifices. The Prefect is my cousin.
The Christians are in the Senate now. They were burned in my grandfather's day. They remember.
When I die, my grandson will be baptised. I know it. I won't watch.
fall: Caecilius Rufus, of the Senate, such as it is. Totila took half of us as hostages. Some didn't come back.
My house on the Caelian has no roof. My sons are dead in the war, one on each side.
Six hundred years of Caecilii. I may be the last one who remembers the name meant anything.
early: Caecilius. My family has given Rome three consuls and a great many dead. Three of my brothers lie at Cannae.
The Senate refused to ransom the prisoners of Cannae. My nephew was among them. I voted with the rest. Rome does not buy back men who surrender.
Now there's Greek silver in the houses, perfume on the young men, and talk of repealing the law that kept our women plain. Victory is more dangerous than Hannibal ever was.
heroic: Caecilius. I have a farm, a seat in the Senate, one silver salt cellar from my grandmother, and it embarrasses me.
I was in the Senate when blind Appius was carried in and told us: no peace with a king in Italy. The old men wept. Then we voted.
Fabricius is my friend. He sent Pyrrhus's traitor doctor back to him in chains, with a note. That's how we fight.
collapse: Caecilius Rufus, of illustrious rank, three titles and no army. The Senate is debating the seating at the games. I have a very good seat.
I paid the Vandals not to burn my house. I paid the new Emperor's general for the right to have paid the Vandals.
Rome is eternal. I say it every morning. My steward has started laughing.

republic: Fabia. Fish. My husband fished, till the river took him. I kept the stall and his debts.
The lender came again. I gave him half. He looked at my daughter. I'll sell the stall before I give him her.
My eldest's married a fisherman. I hope the river's kinder to her than it was to me.
empire: Fabia. Fish, like all the Fabiae on this bank. Widows, most of us. The river takes the men.
Oysters now, from Lake Lucrinus, for the rich. I sell a hundred and eat none.
A child washed up by the bridge. Nobody claimed it. Nobody ever does.
late: Fabia Maria. Baptised at Easter. I still pour wine for the river. It's older than any god.
Fish on the fast days for the Christians. Business has never been better, which tells you something.
The priest says the poor are blessed. The poor would like a word with him.
fall: Maria. The river feeds us now the aqueducts are cut. Fish and water. And the fevers that come with it.
In the siege we ate the fish before they were dead, and then there weren't any.
My grandmother's grandmother sold fish right here. The river doesn't care who rules.
early: Fabia. Fish. My husband rowed in the fleet off Africa. He came home, the gods be thanked, and mends nets now.
Half the women on this bank were widows at Cannae. We kept the stalls. We kept the city fed.
My son wants the fleet too. I'll let him. What else would a Roman boy do?
heroic: Fabia. Fish from the river, and salt from Ostia. My man's with the army. He'll be back for the harvest, he says. They always say.
My mother says the river god likes a good fishwife. I leave him the first fish every morning.
The Greek traders laugh at our little river boats. We'll have ships one day. Big ones.
collapse: Fabia. The Vandal ships came right up the river. I watched them load the gold. It took four days.
Fish is dear now. So is everything. So is nothing, if you've nothing.
My daughter works in the Subura at night. Don't look at me like that.

republic: Stephanus. A freedman. Sit. You'll hear everything worth hearing in this chair, and more that isn't.
The aedile's wife and the gladiator. Everyone knows. The aedile knows. He's paid for the games anyway.
Careful what you say near the man two chairs down. He sells what he hears.
empire: Stephanus, like my father. Same chair. Informers get their hair cut too, so I talk about the weather.
Everyone wants the Emperor's beard. Everyone wants the Emperor's favour. The beard's easier.
A man was taken from that chair last month. Treason, they said. He'd complained about the tax.
late: Stephanus. Same chair, four hundred years, or so I tell people.
The monks want their crowns shaved. They don't tip, and they don't gossip, which is worse.
Stay a while. There are fewer to talk to every year.
early: Menas, barber, from Sicily, like the first barbers in Rome. The Romans only started shaving in my grandfather's time.
The talk in this chair is all Zama and land grants. They're a proud people and they've earned it.
I've lived among Greeks and Carthaginians. These are the ones who keep their word. I'm staying.
heroic: My father was the first barber in Rome, came from Sicily. Before him, the Romans were hairy as bears.
The old senators still won't let me near them. Their beards are the Republic, they say.
Everyone in this chair talks of Pyrrhus. Me, I talk of the price of razors.
